newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia state workers to strike from Feb 11.
newsitem.headline: Colombia state workers to strike from Feb 11.

text.p: Colombia's main public sector unions have declared an indefinite, nationwide strike starting February 11, labor leaders said Monday.
The main private sector unions also back the public sector union's demands, but will not go out on strike immediately, said Wilson Borja, head of the public sector union, FENALTRASE.

The strike aims to paralyze key sectors of the economy, including oil and telecommunications and shut down schools and public offices, Borja said. At least 800,000 workers are affiliated to FENALTRASE.

The legal sector union, which includes judges and magistrates, went on strike Monday. Private sector dock workers have paralyzed operations at the country's main Pacific coast port at Buenaventura, blocking 60 percent of coffee exports and all sugar exports, and National Prison Institute (INPEC) workers were also threatening to strike before February 11.

The state workers are protesting a weighted pay rise of 13.5 percent, despite 1996 inflation of 21.63 percent. Borja said the state workers were also protesting increasingly tough legislation on industrial action and against the state of economic emergency announced by President Ernesto Samper last week.

The full series of economic emergency measures has not yet been announced, but the unions fear the government could cut state jobs and levy value-added tax on a range of basic foodstuffs as it battles to reduce the fiscal deficit by cutting public spending and broadening the tax base.
Borja said the public- and private-sector unions were planning to fix a date for an indefinite, nationwide civic protest in mid-March if the government did not resolve their demands.

"State workers will begin an indefinite strike on February 11. How long that lasts depends on the attitude of the government. We will have a single strike committee and a single negotiating committee in order to maintain solidarity," Borja said.

Labor Minister Orlando Obregon said Monday he would move to declare the current legal-sector strike illegal and said the state workers' strike may also be illegal if it affected essential services, such as health, the water supply and communications.
